scenarios.title: The average that truncates
scenarios.situation: A sensor driver averages integer readings, but the reported average is always rounded down and control decisions drift.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the average lose its fractional part?
choices: Division of two ints is integer division — the fraction is discarded; cast one operand to double before dividing
The function returns int, which rounds to nearest — change the return type to float
C promotes int division to float automatically, but the return truncates — assign to a double first
Integer overflow in sum corrupts the quotient — use long for the accumulator only
scenarios.why: When both operands of / are integers, C performs integer division and discards the remainder — 7/2 is 3, not 3.5. Casting one operand, (double)sum / n, converts the operation to floating-point division before the truncation can happen.
scenarios.hint: What are the types of the two operands of /, and what does that imply about the operation?

scenarios.title: The loop guard that never fires
scenarios.situation: A bounds check meant to reject negative indices instead accepts every value, including -1, leading to an out-of-bounds read.
scenarios.prompt: Why does -1 pass a check against an unsigned size?
choices: The int is converted to size_t (unsigned) for the comparison, so -1 becomes a huge value — compare against (int)n or check i >= 0 first
size_t is signed on 64-bit platforms — the comparison is fine, the bug is elsewhere
C compares the bit patterns directly, and -1 has more bits set
The compiler optimizes the check away at -O2 — build at -O0
scenarios.why: In a mixed signed/unsigned comparison, the usual arithmetic conversions convert the signed operand to the unsigned type. -1 becomes SIZE_MAX, which is greater than any real size, so the guard passes. -Wall's -Wsign-compare warns about exactly this.
scenarios.hint: When one operand is signed and the other unsigned, which type does the comparison actually use?

scenarios.title: The equality that never holds
scenarios.situation: A calibration routine waits for a float to equal exactly 0.1 after repeated additions, but the loop never terminates.
scenarios.prompt: Why is exact float equality unreliable here?
choices: 0.1 has no exact binary representation, so accumulated rounding error makes x slightly off — compare with an epsilon tolerance
float arithmetic is done in double registers, so x is really 1.0 in double — cast to double before comparing
The loop runs 10 times but 0.1f * 10 overflows float precision — use long double
== on floats compares addresses — use memcmp instead
scenarios.why: 0.1 cannot be represented exactly in binary floating point; each addition rounds, and the errors accumulate so x ends up like 1.0000001. The standard practice is fabsf(x - 1.0f) < eps with a small epsilon chosen for the problem's scale.
scenarios.hint: Can 0.1 be written exactly as a finite binary fraction? What happens to the tiny error after ten additions?

scenarios.title: The condition that assigns
scenarios.situation: A success branch that should run when connect_to returns 0 never executes, so every connection attempt looks like a failure.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with the condition?
choices: = assigns 0 to rc, and the condition then tests the assigned value 0, which is false — the branch can never run; the intent was the comparison rc == 0, which -Wall flags via -Wparentheses
rc is uninitialized at the comparison — initialize it to -1
connect_to returns a pointer — compare against NULL instead
C requires parentheses around assignments in conditions — add them
scenarios.why: if (rc = 0) assigns 0 to rc; the condition then tests the value 0, which is false, so the branch never runs (or with a nonzero constant, always runs). The intent was the comparison rc == 0. Compilers warn about this with -Wall (-Wparentheses), and the Yoda style if (0 == rc) makes the typo a compile error.
scenarios.hint: What value does an assignment expression produce, and what does the if statement then test?

scenarios.title: The case that falls through
scenarios.situation: A command dispatcher executes two handlers for a single command, performing an unintended destructive action.
scenarios.prompt: Why did both handlers run?
choices: switch cases fall through by default — the missing break after show_status() lets execution continue into CMD_RESET
CMD_STATUS and CMD_RESET have the same numeric value — renumber the enum
switch compares with assignment — use if/else instead
do_reset is declared static — static functions run for every case
scenarios.why: In C, execution continues from a matched case into the following cases until a break, return, or the switch end. The missing break after show_status() means CMD_STATUS also runs do_reset(). Fallthrough is occasionally intentional (documented with a comment or [[fallthrough]] in C23), but here it is a bug.
scenarios.hint: What stops execution from continuing from one case label into the next?

scenarios.title: The variable that shadows
scenarios.situation: A configuration value set at the top of a function appears unchanged after a block that supposedly updates it.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the update have no effect?
choices: The inner declaration creates a new variable that shadows the outer one — the outer timeout is untouched; -Wshadow warns about this
Inner blocks cannot declare variables in C — this is a compile error being ignored
apply() takes its argument by value so the caller's variable cannot change
timeout is const by default at block scope — remove the inner declaration
scenarios.why: A declaration in an inner block hides (shadows) the outer variable of the same name for the rest of that block. apply(timeout) sees the inner 60, but use(timeout) after the block sees the outer 30. Compiling with -Wshadow surfaces these, and distinct names avoid the confusion entirely.
scenarios.hint: How many distinct variables named timeout exist here, and which one does each statement see?

scenarios.title: The pointer to yesterday's stack
scenarios.situation: A helper builds a formatted message in a local buffer and returns its address. Callers sometimes read garbage.
scenarios.prompt: Why is the returned pointer invalid?
choices: buf is an automatic (stack) variable — its lifetime ends when the function returns, so the pointer dangles
snprintf does not null-terminate — callers read past the buffer
Returning arrays is forbidden in C — return a struct instead
buf is const by default — writing to it is undefined
scenarios.why: Automatic storage duration ends at the closing brace of the block. After make_msg returns, buf's stack space is reused by subsequent calls, so the pointer dangles and reads may show garbage or crash. Correct options: have the caller supply the buffer, return a heap allocation (malloc) with documented ownership, or return a string literal.
scenarios.hint: When does the storage for a local array stop being reserved?

scenarios.title: The allocation that is 8x too small
scenarios.situation: A program allocates an array of 1000 doubles but crashes writing element 200. The allocation call looks plausible at a glance.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with the malloc call?
evidence:
double *a = malloc(1000);  /* 1000 bytes, not 1000 doubles */
for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) a[i] = 0.0;  /* heap overflow */
choices: malloc takes a byte count — 1000 bytes holds only 125 doubles; allocate 1000 * sizeof *a
malloc returns void* and must be cast — the missing cast truncates the pointer
malloc zeroes memory, so the loop is redundant — remove it
1000 exceeds the maximum single malloc on 64-bit — allocate in chunks
scenarios.why: malloc's argument is bytes, not elements. 1000 bytes holds 125 doubles, so writing 1000 doubles overflows the heap — a classic heap buffer overflow. The idiom malloc(n * sizeof *a) sizes by the pointed-to type and stays correct if the type ever changes. (Do not cast malloc's return in C; it can hide a missing #include <stdlib.h>.)
scenarios.hint: What unit does malloc's size argument use — elements, or something else?

scenarios.title: The free that runs twice
scenarios.situation: An error path frees a buffer, then the common cleanup at the function end frees it again. The program crashes intermittently in free().
scenarios.prompt: Why does freeing twice crash, and what is the defensive habit?
choices: Double free corrupts the heap's free-list metadata — set pointers to NULL after freeing, since free(NULL) is a safe no-op
free() can only be called once per program — restructure to a single exit point
malloc'd memory is freed automatically at return — remove all free calls
The crash is from freeing stack memory — buf should be a local array
scenarios.why: Freeing the same allocation twice is undefined behavior: the allocator's bookkeeping gets corrupted, typically crashing later in an unrelated malloc/free. Setting the pointer to NULL immediately after free makes any accidental second free a harmless no-op, since free(NULL) is defined to do nothing.
scenarios.hint: What does the allocator's metadata look like after the same block is released twice? And what does free(NULL) do?

scenarios.title: Off by a factor of four
scenarios.situation: A parser advances an int* by a byte offset to skip a header, but lands in the middle of the data.
scenarios.prompt: How does pointer arithmetic actually scale?
evidence:
int *p = base;
p = p + 16;  /* intended: skip 16 bytes; actually skips 16 ints = 64 bytes */
choices: Adding n to a T* advances by n * sizeof(T) elements — to skip bytes, use a char* or unsigned char*
Pointer addition is in bits — divide the offset by 8 first
p + 16 is byte arithmetic already — the data must be misaligned
Pointer arithmetic on int* is undefined — cast to void* first
scenarios.why: Pointer arithmetic is scaled by the pointed-to type: p + 16 on an int* moves 16 ints forward (64 bytes with 4-byte ints). Byte-level navigation requires a character pointer, since sizeof(char) is 1 by definition. (Arithmetic on void* is a GNU extension, not standard C.)
scenarios.hint: If p points at ints, what does 'one step' mean — one byte, or one int?

scenarios.title: The pointer to nowhere
scenarios.situation: A function declares char *out; writes through it conditionally, and crashes on some runs but not others.
scenarios.prompt: What is the defect, and why is the crash intermittent?
choices: out is uninitialized when v <= 0, holding an indeterminate address — the crash depends on whatever garbage was on the stack
sprintf requires a const destination — declare out as const char*
Local pointers are auto-initialized to NULL — the code should check for NULL
The bug is the missing field width in the format string — use "%8d"
scenarios.why: Automatic variables are not zero-initialized; an uninitialized pointer holds an indeterminate value. Writing through it is undefined behavior — it may crash immediately, corrupt memory silently, or appear to work, depending on the garbage bits. Initializing pointers at declaration (char *out = NULL;) turns the bug into a deterministic, debuggable null dereference.
scenarios.hint: What value does an uninitialized local variable hold, and is it the same on every run?

scenarios.title: The shift that smears
scenarios.situation: A routine shifts array elements left by one to delete an entry, but the tail of the array ends up duplicated instead of shifted.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the copy corrupt overlapping regions, and which function is correct?
choices: memcpy requires non-overlapping regions — use memmove, which handles overlap correctly
memcpy copies backwards — reverse the argument order
The size argument is in elements, not bytes — pass 7
Overlapping copies need strcpy — it handles overlap by contract
scenarios.why: memcpy's contract forbids overlapping source and destination; with overlap the result is undefined and commonly smears because the copy runs front-to-back, overwriting source bytes before they are read. memmove is specified to behave as if the data were copied via a temporary buffer, so it is always safe with overlap.
scenarios.hint: What does the standard guarantee about memcpy when source and destination overlap — and which function makes the opposite guarantee?

scenarios.title: The username that overflowed
scenarios.situation: A login handler copies a username into a 32-byte stack buffer with strcpy. Long usernames corrupt the stack and crash — or worse.
scenarios.prompt: What is the safe replacement for the unbounded copy?
choices: snprintf(user, sizeof user, "%s", name) — always null-terminates and never writes past the buffer
strncpy(user, name, 32) — the classic bounded copy, fully safe as-is
strcpy is fine if you check strlen(name) < 32 first — add the check and keep strcpy
memcpy(user, name, 32) — copies exactly the buffer size
scenarios.why: strcpy copies until the null terminator with no length limit — a textbook stack buffer overflow. snprintf with the buffer size always null-terminates and truncates safely. (strncpy is a trap here: it does not null-terminate when the source is too long, leaving a non-terminated string.)
scenarios.hint: Which function takes the destination size and guarantees a terminating null byte no matter what?

scenarios.title: The string with no end
scenarios.situation: A hand-built message buffer prints trailing garbage because the terminator was never written.
scenarios.prompt: What defines the end of a C string, and what went wrong?
choices: C strings end at the first '\0' — the loop filled all 16 bytes with 'A' and never stored a terminator, so printf overruns
printf("%s") stops at the buffer size — the loop should fill only 15 bytes
char arrays are auto-terminated on declaration — the bug is the loop bound
%s prints exactly 16 bytes for a char[16] — the garbage comes from uninitialized printf state
scenarios.why: A C string is a convention, not a type: characters up to and including the first null byte. The loop wrote sixteen 'A's with no '\0', so printf keeps reading into adjacent memory until it happens to find a zero byte — a buffer over-read. Always reserve one byte for the terminator.
scenarios.hint: How does printf("%s") know where the string ends?

scenarios.title: sizeof lies inside the function
scenarios.situation: A helper computes an array's length with sizeof(arr)/sizeof(arr[0]), but inside the function it always yields 2 on a 64-bit machine.
scenarios.prompt: Why does sizeof give the wrong answer here?
choices: The array parameter decays to a pointer — sizeof(arr) is the pointer size (8), not the array size; pass the length as a separate argument
sizeof is evaluated at runtime and the array is heap-allocated — use strlen instead
int arr[] declares a variable-length array — its size is unknown until called
Division of sizeof values truncates — cast to double first
scenarios.why: Function parameters declared as arrays are adjusted to pointers — the function receives only an address, with no length information. sizeof(arr) is therefore sizeof(int*). The robust pattern is to pass the element count alongside the pointer, or use a struct wrapping both.
scenarios.hint: What does the function actually receive — the array, or something smaller?

scenarios.title: The comparison that compares addresses
scenarios.situation: A command parser checks if the input equals "quit" with ==, but typing quit never exits.
scenarios.prompt: Why does == fail for strings?
choices: == on char* compares pointer addresses, not string contents — use strcmp(line, "quit") == 0 (and strip the newline from fgets)
String literals are immutable — copy "quit" into a buffer before comparing
== works only for single chars — compare line[0] == 'q'
fgets includes the newline — the comparison fails on content, not on == semantics
scenarios.why: Applied to pointers, == tests whether they point to the same address. line and the literal "quit" are different objects, so the comparison is always false regardless of contents. strcmp compares character by character and returns 0 for equal strings. (Also note: fgets retains the '\n', so real code must strip it first — but the == itself is the conceptual bug.)
scenarios.hint: What are the operands of == here — characters, or addresses of characters?

scenarios.title: The transposed image
scenarios.situation: A grayscale image stored as a flat row-major array renders transposed — rows and columns are swapped.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct index formula for element (r, c) in a row-major WxH array?
choices: px[r * w + c] — each row occupies w consecutive elements, so row r starts at offset r*w
px[c * h + r] — column-major is the C default for flat arrays
px[r + c] — rows and columns are interchangeable in flat storage
px[(r + c) * w] — the stride applies to the sum of indices
scenarios.why: C lays out multidimensional data in row-major order: row r begins after r full rows, i.e., at offset r*w, and column c is c elements into that row. Swapping to c*w + r effectively transposes the image. (Column-major, c*h + r, is Fortran's convention, not C's.)
scenarios.hint: In memory, which elements sit next to each other — elements of the same row, or the same column?

scenarios.title: The function you must never call
scenarios.situation: Legacy code reads a line with gets(buf). A security audit flags it as a critical finding regardless of buffer size.
scenarios.prompt: Why is gets() unfixable, and what replaces it?
evidence:
char buf[128];
gets(buf);  /* removed from C11: cannot be used safely */
choices: gets() takes no size argument, so no caller can prevent overflow — use fgets(buf, sizeof buf, stdin) and strip the newline
gets() is merely deprecated — it is safe for buffers over 1 KB
gets() fails on empty input — check feof() before calling it
The fix is scanf("%s") — it stops at whitespace, bounding the input
scenarios.why: gets() cannot know the buffer size — that information is simply not passed — so any input longer than the buffer overflows. It was removed from the C standard in C11. fgets takes the size, always null-terminates, and reads at most size-1 characters; the retained newline is stripped explicitly.
scenarios.hint: What parameter would a safe version of gets() need — and does gets() have it?

scenarios.title: The struct that is bigger than its parts
scenarios.situation: A wire-protocol struct with a char, an int, and a short measures 12 bytes instead of the expected 7, breaking a binary file format.
scenarios.prompt: Why is the struct larger than the sum of its members?
evidence:
struct pkt { char tag; int seq; short len; };
printf("%zu\n", sizeof(struct pkt));  /* 12, not 7 */
choices: The compiler inserts padding so each member meets its alignment requirement — reorder members largest-first or serialize field by field
sizeof counts the struct name — use sizeof on an instance instead
char promotes to int inside structs — declare tag as int
The struct includes a hidden vtable pointer — C structs always carry one
scenarios.why: Members must be aligned to their natural boundaries (int on a 4-byte boundary), so the compiler inserts padding bytes — here 3 after tag and 2 at the end, totaling 12. Never memcpy a struct to the wire; padding bytes are indeterminate and layouts vary by platform. Serialize each field explicitly or reorder by decreasing size to minimize padding.
scenarios.hint: At what addresses must the int member sit, and what has to fill the gaps before it?

scenarios.title: The crash on a missing file
scenarios.situation: A tool segfaults when the input file does not exist, instead of printing a clean error.
scenarios.prompt: What check is missing after fopen?
choices: fopen returns NULL on failure — check for NULL and report the error (perror/strerror with errno) before using the stream
fopen never fails for mode "r" — the crash is in fgets with an uninitialized buffer
Missing files raise SIGSEGV by design — install a signal handler
fopen needs the "r+" mode to test existence — "r" assumes the file exists
scenarios.why: fopen signals failure by returning NULL, and passing NULL to fgets is undefined behavior — typically a segfault. The mandatory pattern is if (!f) { perror(path); exit/return; }. errno (with perror or strerror) tells you why: ENOENT for missing files, EACCES for permissions.
scenarios.hint: What does fopen return when the open fails, and what happens when that value reaches fgets?

scenarios.title: The short read nobody noticed
scenarios.situation: A file loader reads fixed-size records with fread but processes garbage when the file is truncated mid-record.
scenarios.prompt: How do you detect a short read?
choices: Check fread's return value — it reports items actually read; a value less than requested means EOF or error (distinguish with feof/ferror)
fread throws an exception on short reads — wrap it in a signal handler
Call fseek(f, 0, SEEK_END) first to guarantee the file is long enough
Short reads cannot happen on regular files — the file must be a pipe
scenarios.why: fread returns the number of complete items read, which can be less than requested at end-of-file or on I/O error. Ignoring it means processing uninitialized or stale memory. The return check plus feof()/ferror() distinguishes clean EOF from a real error.
scenarios.hint: What does fread return, and what does it mean when that number is smaller than what you asked for?

scenarios.title: The file that grew on Windows
scenarios.situation: A binary dumper writes bytes with fopen(path, "w") and the output is corrupt on Windows but fine on Linux.
scenarios.prompt: What does text mode do to byte streams, and how do you stop it?
evidence:
FILE *f = fopen("out.bin", "w");  /* text mode on Windows */
fwrite(data, 1, n, f);  /* 0x0A bytes become 0x0D 0x0A */
choices: In text mode the runtime translates '\n' to CR-LF on write — open binary files with "wb" (and "rb" for reading)
Windows fwrite is limited to text — use the Win32 WriteFile API instead
The corruption is from Unicode normalization — set the locale to C
"w" truncates but also compresses the stream — use "a" to append raw bytes
scenarios.why: Text-mode streams may translate newline characters (and on some systems treat Ctrl-Z as EOF). For binary data that translation corrupts bytes. Opening with "wb"/"rb" selects binary mode, where bytes pass through untouched. On POSIX the modes are identical, which is why the bug only appears on Windows.
scenarios.hint: Which byte value gets expanded in text mode on Windows, and which fopen mode disables the translation?

scenarios.title: The union that forgets its type
scenarios.situation: A message struct uses a union for payload variants, but readers interpret an int payload as a float after a refactor changed which variant was written.
scenarios.prompt: What discipline makes unions safe?
choices: Pair the union with a tag enum recording which member is active — a tagged (discriminated) union — and check the tag before reading
Unions auto-track their active member — the reader has a stale binary
Cast through void* to reinterpret safely — the bug is the direct member access
Unions are deprecated — replace with three separate structs
scenarios.why: A union overlays all members on the same storage; the language does not remember which was written last. Reading a different member than was written reinterprets the bits (type punning) — occasionally intended, usually a bug. A tag enum set alongside every write, checked on every read, makes the active variant explicit.
scenarios.hint: All union members share the same bytes. What record tells the reader which interpretation is valid?

scenarios.title: Measuring a file with fseek
scenarios.situation: A loader needs a file's size to allocate a buffer. A teammate proposes fseek to the end and ftell.
scenarios.prompt: How do you get a file's size portably, and what is the caveat of the fseek/ftell trick?
choices: fseek/ftell works for binary streams, but ftell returns long (not 64-bit everywhere) — for large files prefer fstat/fileno or stat() with off_t
ftell returns the size directly without fseek — the fseek is redundant
SEEK_END is undefined for regular files — read the whole file counting bytes
stat() cannot see open files — the fseek/ftell approach is the only portable one
scenarios.why: Seeking to SEEK_END then ftell gives the size for binary streams, but long may be 32 bits (Windows, many 32-bit ABIs), overflowing past 2 GB. The robust route is fstat() on fileno(f) (POSIX) or _fstat64, reading st_size as an off_t/64-bit value — no seeking required.
scenarios.hint: What type does ftell return, and how wide is that type on a 32-bit long platform?

scenarios.title: The macro that does bad math
scenarios.situation: SQUARE(1+2) evaluates to 5 instead of 9, and a max macro with side effects evaluates its argument twice.
scenarios.prompt: What are the two classic function-like macro pitfalls, and how do you avoid them?
evidence:
#define SQUARE(x) x * x
int a = SQUARE(1 + 2);  /* 1 + 2 * 1 + 2 = 5 */
choices: Missing parentheses around parameters and the whole body — write #define SQUARE(x) ((x) * (x)); for side-effect safety prefer a static inline function
Macros cannot take expressions — only pass simple variables to SQUARE
The preprocessor evaluates right-to-left — reverse the operand order
#define constants are typed — declare SQUARE as returning int
scenarios.why: Macros are pure textual substitution: SQUARE(1+2) expands to 1+2*1+2 = 5. Parenthesizing every parameter use and the entire body fixes precedence. The deeper fix for double evaluation (SQUARE(i++) increments twice) is a static inline function, which evaluates arguments once and is type-checked.
scenarios.hint: What does the preprocessor actually do with SQUARE(1+2) — compute, or substitute text?

scenarios.title: The header included twice
scenarios.situation: A struct definition in a header triggers 'redefinition' errors when two other headers both include it.
scenarios.prompt: How do you make a header safe to include multiple times?
evidence: struct point { int x; int y; };  /* no guard: included via a.h and b.h -> error */
choices: Wrap the header in an include guard (#ifndef TYPES_H / #define / #endif) or #pragma once
Headers must only be included once per project — remove one of the includes
Mark the struct static so each inclusion gets its own copy
Move the struct definition into a .c file and extern it in the header
scenarios.why: Headers are textually pasted into each translation unit, so without a guard the struct is defined twice and the compiler rejects the redefinition. An include guard (or the widely supported #pragma once) makes repeated inclusion a no-op. Guards belong in every header as a matter of hygiene.
scenarios.hint: What does #include literally do, and what happens when the same definition text appears twice?

scenarios.title: The linker says 'multiple definition'
scenarios.situation: A global config variable is defined in a header included by two .c files. Each compiles fine, but linking fails.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the linker complain, and how should globals be shared?
evidence: /usr/bin/ld: main.o: multiple definition of `log_level'; util.o: first defined here
choices: Each translation unit gets its own definition — declare extern int log_level; in the header and define it in exactly one .c file
Headers cannot declare variables — move log_level into main.c only
The linker needs --allow-multiple-definition for shared globals
Make it static in the header so each file gets an independent copy
scenarios.why: A bare int log_level; in a header is a tentative definition in every translation unit that includes it, violating the one-definition rule at link time. The pattern is: extern declaration in the header (a promise it exists somewhere) plus a single definition in one .c file. (static in the header would instead create separate independent variables per file — usually not what you want.)
scenarios.hint: How many definitions of log_level exist after two .c files include the header — and how many should there be?

scenarios.title: The helper that collided
scenarios.situation: Two .c files each define a static-less helper named hash(). Linking fails with a duplicate symbol.
scenarios.prompt: How do you keep a helper private to its translation unit?
evidence: int hash(const char *s) { ... }  /* collision at link */
choices: Declare them static — static at file scope gives internal linkage, so each file's hash is invisible to the linker
Rename one of them — C has no namespacing mechanism
Put both in a header as static inline so the linker merges them
Compile with -fvisibility=hidden to hide all symbols
scenarios.why: File-scope functions default to external linkage: one global namespace across the whole program. static restricts a function (or variable) to internal linkage — visible only within its translation unit — which both prevents collisions and documents that the helper is private.
scenarios.hint: What is the default visibility of a file-scope function, and which keyword narrows it?

scenarios.title: Debug logging that ships
scenarios.situation: Verbose debug prints guarded by a runtime flag still cost string formatting in release builds and leak internal details to logs.
scenarios.prompt: How do you compile debug code out of release builds entirely?
choices: Guard with #ifdef DEBUG and compile release with DEBUG undefined — the preprocessor removes the code completely, zero runtime cost
Runtime flags are sufficient — the branch predictor makes the check free
Use assert() for debug logging — -O removes it automatically
Comment out the debug lines before release — automation is unreliable
scenarios.why: Conditional compilation removes the debug code during preprocessing, so release binaries contain no trace of it — no formatting cost, no leaked internals, no binary bloat. A runtime if (debug) still evaluates arguments and ships the strings. Build systems typically add -DDEBUG to debug builds only.
scenarios.hint: Which runs first — the preprocessor or the program? Which one can make code vanish from the binary?

scenarios.title: The warning nobody read
scenarios.situation: A sign-conversion bug shipped because the build ran without warnings enabled. The compiler had flagged it all along.
scenarios.prompt: Which flags turn the compiler into a bug-finding ally?
evidence: cc -O2 -o app main.c util.c  # no warning flags
choices: Compile with -Wall -Wextra (and -Werror in CI) plus -g for debuggability — warnings catch sign issues, unused results, and shadowing before they ship
-O3 implies all warnings — just raise the optimization level
Warnings are stylistic noise — rely on runtime testing instead
-pedantic alone enables every useful warning
scenarios.why: -Wall -Wextra enable the high-signal warnings (sign comparison, implicit conversions, unused variables, missing prototypes). -Werror in CI turns them into build failures so they cannot be ignored. -g adds debug info with negligible cost. Optimization level does not control diagnostics — that is a common misconception.
scenarios.hint: Which flags ask the compiler to report suspicious code, and which one refuses to build when it finds any?

scenarios.title: Segfault with no obvious cause
scenarios.situation: A program segfaults in production. A core dump exists, but nobody knows which line crashed.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fastest way to find the crashing line from the core dump?
evidence:
$ gdb ./app core
(gdb) bt
#0  0x... in render (ctx=0x0) at render.c:42
#1  0x... in main at main.c:17
choices: Load the core in gdb and run bt (backtrace) — frame #0 shows the crashing function, file, and line; build with -g for symbols
Add printfs and re-run until the crash reproduces — core dumps contain no line information
Run strings on the core dump and search for the function name
Core dumps only record the signal — recompile at -O0 and hope it crashes again
scenarios.why: A core dump is a snapshot of the crashed process's memory, including the call stack. gdb's bt prints every frame with function names and line numbers (when built with -g). Frame #0 is the crash site — here a NULL ctx dereferenced at render.c:42. No reproduction needed.
scenarios.hint: What does a core dump actually contain, and which gdb command prints the call stack?

scenarios.title: The overflow valgrind missed in CI time
scenarios.situation: A heap buffer overflow passes all tests but corrupts data in long runs. The team wants a fast automated check in CI.
scenarios.prompt: Which tool catches memory errors at runtime with minimal setup?
evidence:
cc -fsanitize=address,undefined -g -o test_app *.c
./test_app  # aborts with stack trace on first memory error
choices: AddressSanitizer (+ UBSan) — compiler-inserted checks abort with a precise stack trace on overflows, use-after-free, and UB
valgrind --tool=memcheck — the only tool that finds heap overflows
-Wall at compile time — it detects all runtime memory errors statically
Electric Fence — the modern standard for CI memory checking
scenarios.why: AddressSanitizer instruments every memory access at compile time, catching heap/stack/global overflows and use-after-free with exact stack traces, at roughly 2x slowdown — fast enough for CI. UBSan adds checks for signed overflow, bad shifts, and misaligned access. Valgrind needs no rebuild but is 10-50x slower.
scenarios.hint: Which approach inserts the checks at compile time so the instrumented binary reports the exact offending line?

scenarios.title: The log line that never appeared
scenarios.situation: Debug prints to stdout vanish when the program crashes, while prints to stderr survive. The team is confused about which output to trust.
scenarios.prompt: Why does stdout lose the last lines on a crash?
choices: stdout is block-buffered when redirected (line-buffered on a terminal); buffered data is lost on abnormal termination — stderr is unbuffered by default
printf is asynchronous — it returns before writing anything
stderr bypasses the filesystem — it writes directly to the disk controller
The crash corrupts the stdout buffer — always call sync() before risky code
scenarios.why: stdio buffers stdout (line-buffered to terminals, fully buffered to files/pipes) for performance; on _exit/abort/crash the buffer is never flushed, so trailing output is lost. stderr is unbuffered by default, making it the right stream for diagnostics. fflush(stdout) before risky calls, or setvbuf for explicit control.
scenarios.hint: Where do printf's bytes sit between the call and the actual write — and what happens to them on a crash?

scenarios.title: The loop that writes one past the end
scenarios.situation: A buffer fill loop uses <= against the size, corrupting the byte after the buffer. It passes tests because the corruption usually lands on padding.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct loop bound idiom?
evidence:
char buf[64];
for (int i = 0; i <= 64; i++) buf[i] = 0;  /* writes buf[64]: out of bounds */
choices: Use i < 64 (half-open range) — valid indices are 0..63, and < size is the canonical bound
Use i <= 63 — equivalent but less idiomatic
Declare buf[65] so the <= loop stays in bounds
Off-by-one writes are harmless on the stack — the red zone absorbs them
scenarios.why: Valid indices for buf[64] are 0 through 63. The idiom for (i = 0; i < N; i++) iterates exactly N times over exactly the valid range — the half-open [0, N) convention used across C and its stdlib. <= N iterates N+1 times and writes one past the end, which is undefined behavior even when it appears harmless.
scenarios.hint: How many valid indices does buf[64] have, and how many iterations does <= 64 perform?

scenarios.title: The counter that starts at garbage
scenarios.situation: A tally variable is declared but not initialized. Totals are wrong by a random amount on every run.
scenarios.prompt: Why must automatic variables be initialized explicitly?
evidence:
int total;  /* indeterminate value */
for (...) total += x;  /* adds onto garbage */
choices: Automatic variables have indeterminate values — reading one before assignment is undefined behavior; initialize at declaration (int total = 0;)
The compiler zero-initializes locals at -O2 — build optimized to fix it
Integers default to 1 in C — subtract 1 after the loop
The bug is += on a declaration — use total = total + x instead
scenarios.why: Unlike static storage (zero-initialized), automatic variables start with whatever bits were on the stack — reading them is undefined behavior, and -Wmaybe-uninitialized / -Wuninitialized warn about it. Initializing at declaration is free, obvious, and eliminates the entire bug class.
scenarios.hint: What value does a local variable hold before your code assigns one — and is the compiler required to pick any particular value?

scenarios.title: The invariant nobody checked
scenarios.situation: A parser assumes its index never exceeds the buffer length, but a malformed input violates the assumption deep in the code, far from where the bad index originated.
scenarios.prompt: How do you catch violated assumptions at their source during development?
choices: assert() documents and checks invariants — it aborts with file/line at the exact violation in debug builds, and NDEBUG compiles it out for release
assert() is for user input validation — it stays active in release builds
Assertions slow down parsing — replace with comments describing the invariant
assert fires only in gdb — run every test under the debugger
scenarios.why: assert() turns 'this must be true here' into executable documentation: in debug builds a violation aborts immediately at the source with the file and line, instead of corrupting state that crashes pages later. Defining NDEBUG (typical for release) compiles asserts away for zero cost. It is for internal invariants, not for validating external input.
scenarios.hint: Where do you want to learn about a violated assumption — at the moment it breaks, or three function calls later?

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you tracked down a memory corruption bug (overflow, use-after-free, leak).
points: Symptoms and how you reproduced it
pitfalls: Vague 'I looked at the code' with no tooling

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to debug without being able to reproduce the issue locally.
points: What evidence you had (cores, logs, traces)
How you reasoned from the evidence
The fix and how you gained confidence without a repro

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a disagreement over a low-level design choice (memory ownership, error handling, API shape).
pitfalls: Framing the other side as careless

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you improved the safety or reliability of existing C code.
points: The change (bounds checks, sanitizers, safer APIs)
pitfalls: Cosmetic changes framed as safety work

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you had to learn a new toolchain, platform, or ABI constraint quickly.
points: How you got up to speed

behavioral.prompt: Describe a production incident involving native code. What was your role in the response?
pitfalls: Claiming sole credit for team work

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you received tough feedback in a code review. How did you handle it?
points: What changed in your code or habits

behavioral.prompt: Describe a situation where you had to balance performance against correctness or safety.
pitfalls: Choosing speed with no safety analysis
